title: Gate Editor: real populations, reversible views and exact exports
description: Draw gates on downloaded cell measurements, verify saved membership, compare real three-dimensional and projected views, and inspect bounded clustering without inventing biological labels.
objectives: Load real measurements and distinguish gates, view filters and visibility.
Save and restore feature boundaries, then export membership with exact object identities.
Explore three-dimensional bounds and principal components without confusing a projection with a reusable fitted transform.
Compare actual cluster-search outcomes and use the local measurement console.
prerequisite: Download the Annotate example first, then make a private copy of its measurements database. Gate Editor has no separate example-download button. This recording uses all 2,341 real cell rows and modifies only that private copy when exporting; tutorial gate names are inspection labels, not biological ground truth.

scenes.narration: Open Gate Editor in Home's Tools category. Drag the dividers to give the plot, gate table and side controls enough room. This lesson uses the downloaded Annotate measurements; Gate Editor does not have its own example-download button.

Use Load table to open a private copy of measurements dot D B. Choose the cell table: this example contains two thousand three hundred and forty-one real objects. Export gates writes to a database, so keep the original example unchanged and work on the copy.

Choose cell area for X and cell channel one mean intensity for Y, with the Rectangle tool. Each point represents a measured object. Inspect the feature names and units before drawing; an area-intensity region alone does not establish an infected cell or another biological class.

Drag across the scatter, release and enter a descriptive gate name. Our tutorial population is deliberately an inspection example. The shape records numerical boundaries in these two measurements; it is not a model trained to recognise cells from their images.

This drawn region contains six hundred and fifty-five objects, about twenty-eight percent of the table. Read the count and percentages beside the gate name. Different mouse positions produce different boundaries and counts, so use the saved strategy when you need an exact repeat.

Unticking the gate hides its overlay without deleting its definition or changing membership. Tick it again to restore the view. This is different from Delete gate, and different from the Filter tab, which changes the objects displayed beneath the gates.

Use Save gates to keep the named feature boundaries in a JSON strategy. Here we save, actually delete the gate, and then load the saved file. Reusing a strategy requires matching measurement names, units and preprocessing, not simply a table with the same number of columns.

Load gates restores the same boundaries and all six hundred and fifty-five members. We checked membership after actually deleting and reloading the gate, rather than merely saving a file. On another dataset, verify the restored boundaries and object identities before relying on its counts.

Save graph writes the actual figure; this recording's preferences produce a PNG and a PDF. A figure is different from a gate strategy or exported membership. Keep the corresponding data and strategy when you need to reproduce how a displayed population was defined.

Export gates writes membership flags to the private database's filters table. Our first gate marks exactly six hundred and fifty-five cell identities, matched by plate, row, column, field, object label and object type. The original download and underlying cell measurements remain unchanged.

Draw a second shape while the first is selected. Its two hundred and fifty-nine objects include some outside the first: new drawing is not automatically nested, despite older status wording. Save this two-gate strategy separately and inspect any parent relationships explicitly when loading an existing hierarchy.

Choose three D and cell perimeter for Z to inspect three actual measurements. The spin-axis buttons guide rotation. Rotating changes the view, not the saved boundaries of the two existing area-intensity gates; return to two D to inspect those shapes again.

From view creates a named box with bounds on all three displayed measurements. Our full-volume example includes every loaded object: it demonstrates the control, not an enriched biological population. Save the three-gate strategy separately so the earlier two-gate file remains available.

The x D toggle computes principal components from eligible measurements. It is separate from the two D or three D view choice. Here the source label reports seventeen, thirteen and six percent explained variance for the first three components; these are variance fractions, not classification accuracy.

Turning x D off retains the component columns; choose the raw axes again when returning to raw-feature gates. A saved gate strategy does not save the fitted projection. Component names alone do not make independently fitted projections compatible, so do not reuse their gate boundaries blindly.

For Search, widen the side panel and remove the temporary gates after saving them. Use the same two raw features, scaling enabled, twenty minimum neighbours and five Walk steps. Run walk opens a confirmation in this build; check that its values match the visible controls.

The actual Walk selects a radius near zero point one six seven and reports two populations, with thirty-three percent of objects outside them. Inspect the resulting outlines. Density clustering and its saved polygon gates are exploratory descriptions, not validated cell types or proof that excluded objects are invalid.

Save the Walk strategy, remove its temporary gates, turn Walk off and run radius zero point five. This separate choice creates one larger polygon gate, containing two thousand two hundred and thirty-nine objects. It is not a better answer merely because it includes more cells.

Reload the saved two-gate raw-feature strategy, then add cell area in Filter. Setting the lower cutoff to twenty-one thousand nine hundred and twenty-five leaves one thousand one hundred and seventy-one displayed objects. This live preview narrows the view without rewriting the saved gate boundaries.

Clear the filter and all two thousand three hundred and forty-one objects return. Check both the active view filter and the gate definition before interpreting counts or exporting. Hiding an overlay, filtering a view and deleting a gate are three different operations.

Drag the far-right divider left to reveal the console. Enter len, open parenthesis, D F, close parenthesis: the real table returns two thousand three hundred and forty-one. The expression console works locally; it is not an answer generated by an artificial-intelligence model.

The chat box is separate from expressions. We leave an unsent draft, without demonstrating an assistant or biological interpretation. In Python, GateSet from spacr.qt.widgets.gate_spec stores definitions; gate_mask_over_table and export_gate in spacr.filters evaluate and save full-table object flags. Verify the identities before downstream annotation.
